title: Lech Lecha: be a blessing (Genesis 12:2)
hook: Abram is told not only to be blessed but "be thou a blessing"

segments.voice: Yesterday, lech lecha: go, to you, a road outward and a road inward. Your line was go to yourself. Did you take the walk alone? Now, the very next verse. Day one hundred seventy-two.

People say it all the time now, sometimes with a hashtag: so blessed. A new job, a vacation photo, a good cup of coffee. Hashtag blessed. It means: good things came to me. And that's real; gratitude is good. But notice where the blessing stops. It lands on you, and there it stays. Right after God tells Abram to go, God makes him a string of promises. A great nation. Blessing. A great name. And then, at the end, a short phrase that turns the whole thing around. Today, the phrase that sends the blessing out the door.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `IT LANDS ON YOU, AND STAYS.` → `A PHRASE THAT TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: The verse: "And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing." Be thou a blessing. In Hebrew, veheyeh bracha. And grammatically it's an imperative. Not a prediction. Not, you'll turn out to be a blessing. A command: be one. Abram isn't only a place where blessing arrives. He's supposed to be a place where it flows out. The next verse makes it wider: "and in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed." All the families. Not only his own. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, reads a handover here. He says: until now, blessings were in God's hands. God blessed Adam, God blessed Noah. From now on, God tells Abram, the blessings are given into your hands. You bless whomever you want. In this reading, a human being is trusted with blessing. And the word itself, bracha, may already be familiar. It's the name for what Jews say over bread, over wine, over a new season. Every one of those blessings is said by a person. In Rashi's reading, that human work of blessing starts here, with Abram. And the portion shows you what it looks like. In a few chapters Abram will throw open his tent to three strangers and run to feed them. He'll argue with God to save a city that isn't his. Being blessed is something that happens to you. Being a blessing is something you do.
screen: `I WILL BLESS THEE.` · `VEHEYEH BRACHA: A COMMAND.` · `THE BLESSINGS, NOW IN YOUR HANDS.` · `BRACHA: OVER BREAD, OVER WINE.` · then, large: `BE A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one blessing flow out. Settle, and breathe. First, name one good thing that's come to you lately, small is fine. Let yourself feel blessed by it. Then ask: who could use some of this? Picture one person. Imagine the good thing overflowing, like water over the edge of a pool, and reaching them. Plan one small way to pass it on today. The bell holds the time.
Lech Lecha. The portion where Abram sets out, and is told not only I will bless thee, but be thou a blessing.
Your line: be a blessing. Today, do one thing that makes someone else's day better, and don't mention it. Day one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often read 'be thou a blessing' as a charge to every Jew to bring good into the world, and the verse is frequently quoted in sermons on this portion and at life-cycle events.

fork.setup: you're Abram. God has promised you a great nation, blessing and a great name. what's the last thing God says in that verse?
fork.reveal: "and be thou a blessing." the blessing isn't meant to stop with you.

original.note: Hebrew: a blessing; also the word for what Jews say over bread, wine and a new season.

trapdoor: what you thought: blessed means good things happened to you.
what it means: Abram is told to be a blessing: a place blessing flows out from, for all the families of the earth.
what a scholar hears: veheyeh bracha (12:2) as an imperative; Rashi on 12:2 from Genesis Rabbah 39:11, the blessings given into Abram's hand.
